title: Top-down analysis of path compression
formal: The saved source proposes a simpler direct derivation of the inverse-Ackermann path-compression bound from the Seidel–Sharir recurrence using a classical Ackermann definition. The asymptotic bound itself is already proved. This is retained as an expository research note, not an unresolved complexity claim.
context:
Path compression is a standard operation in disjoint-set data structures: a find follows parent pointers to a representative and redirects the visited nodes toward that representative. Its analysis explains why some union-find algorithms have a running time involving a very slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function.

Seidel and Sharir provide a top-down analysis based on recurrences. The seminar note seeks a more direct connection between that analysis and a classical definition of Ackermann’s function. A clearer derivation could be valuable for teaching and for transferring the method to other settings.

That motivation does not make the saved request a precise conjecture about an unknown bound. Different readers may disagree about which proof is simple or direct, and the source does not supply a formal condition that would resolve the disagreement. This review therefore retains the bibliography and motivation while removing the record from the unfinished open-question queue. It does not assert that no improved exposition is possible, nor that the requested exposition has been written.
why: Retained for its connection to a fundamental amortized-analysis technique. It is excluded from the open-problem selection because the saved success criterion is expository and subjective, whereas the underlying asymptotic guarantee is known.
status_note: The source asks for a simpler direct proof of an already established inverse-Ackermann bound. It does not specify a proof system, proof-length threshold, or other objective criterion for simplicity. It therefore does not satisfy this catalogue’s requirement that an open question have an unambiguous mathematical resolution.

title: Bit-complexity guarantees in extensions of word RAM
formal: Model proposal: augment a w-bit word RAM with constant-cost evaluation of Boolean functions on O(w) input bits that have circuits of depth O(log w) and size O(w^2). The source motivates adopting this convention; it does not specify a proposition whose truth is unknown.
context:
A machine model determines which operations are charged as elementary steps. The word RAM usually treats several arithmetic and bitwise operations on an entire word as constant-time instructions. An analysis in that model can therefore count a multiplication as one step even though implementing it at the bit level requires a circuit with many gates.

Even’s proposal uses circuit size and depth to describe a broader class of candidate instructions. The motivation is to make the computational convention less dependent on which particular operations happen to be listed, and to avoid long simulations using the standard instruction set. This is a substantive modeling idea that can affect the interpretation of data-structure bounds.

The seminar entry nevertheless supplies no theorem to prove or refute about the proposed model. For example, an equivalence with the ordinary word RAM would be a separate question requiring explicit circuit uniformity, instruction-family, and simulation-cost conventions. The source does not fix that question, and this catalogue should not attribute it to the author by inference. The record is retained as background for model-sensitive questions, with an individual disposition rather than a fabricated open statement.
why: Retained because the cost of word operations is fundamental to interpreting algorithmic speedups. Excluded from the open-problem selection because defining or advocating a model is not itself an unresolved proposition with an objective answer criterion.
status_note: The source proposes an extended instruction set for the word RAM. It does not pose a quantified claim about algorithms, simulation overhead, or lower bounds. The saved label should therefore not be presented as a well-defined unresolved mathematical problem.

progress.text: Even proposes admitting instructions according to bounded-depth, bounded-size Boolean circuits and gives motivations for the extension. The source does not state an open simulation theorem.

title: Local computation of MIS with polynomial degree dependence — resolved
formal: Does there exist a randomized local computation algorithm which, for every n-vertex simple undirected graph of maximum degree at most Δ, answers whether any requested vertex belongs to one consistently chosen maximal independent set, using at most C(Δ+1)^a(log(n+1))^b graph probes per answer? Here C,a,b are absolute constants, and with probability at least 1−1/n all n answers are jointly correct and meet the probe bound. The answer is yes, by Ghaffari’s FOCS 2022 result.
definitions: Take n≥2, vertex names [n], and 0≤Δ≤n−1, with n and Δ supplied. A probe (u,i), for u∈[n] and 1≤i≤Δ+1, returns u’s i-th neighbor in a fixed arbitrary ordering, or a null symbol if i exceeds its degree. The input is static; no preprocessing may inspect the graph for free. The algorithm can probe any vertex name, not only neighbors of the requested vertex. It uses shared randomness fixed independently of the graph, and its answer for a vertex is independent of the order, repetition, or presence of other vertex requests. With that randomness fixed, let I be the set of vertices receiving answer 1. Success requires that no edge has both endpoints in I and every vertex outside I has a neighbor in I. Local computation between probes is not charged here. The probability is over the shared randomness, for each fixed graph; it must control all vertices simultaneously. The original 2019 question uses one whole-neighbor-list query as its unit. The two access conventions differ by at most a factor Δ+1, so they have the same polynomial-in-Δ target.
answer_criterion: A globally consistent algorithm with the stated polynomial probe bound answers the historical question affirmatively; such an algorithm is now known. A bound averaged over a uniformly random requested vertex would not have sufficed. Optimizing the polynomial exponent is a further question, not an unresolved part of the existence statement retained here.
context:
A maximal independent set can contain a linear number of vertices. In a large implicit graph, a user may need only the membership of one vertex and have no reason to generate the entire set. An LCA supplies that membership on demand. Different answers must nevertheless describe one valid global solution: independently choosing a convenient set for each request could select both endpoints of an edge.

The target is maximality under inclusion, not maximum cardinality. A globally run greedy algorithm already computes a maximal independent set efficiently. The local difficulty is reconstructing the requested decision without following a chain of dependencies through a large part of the graph. Reusing fixed randomness allows separate requests to refer to the same implicit computation.

The degree dependence is central. A bound with an exponent growing as log log Δ is much larger than a fixed polynomial when Δ grows. The 2019 workshop question asks to remove that growing exponent while keeping dependence on n polylogarithmic. Its archived wording still presents this as an open question.

The 2022 algorithm resolves that target by carefully limiting which parts of a randomized distributed computation must be explored. Directly expanding a whole neighborhood for every simulated round is too expensive; controlling the actual dependencies is what permits a fixed polynomial in Δ. The remaining sparse components can then be completed consistently.

This resolved card stays in the catalogue to correct the inherited status and preserve its history. It also provides a useful reference point for more demanding targets, such as a linear or quadratic dependence on Δ. Those strengthen the question and should receive their own precise formulation and source if included.
why: Historically this asked whether a basic graph symmetry-breaking task can be answered locally with efficient dependence on both degree and graph size. Its resolution is fundamental to the LCA model and supports local algorithms for matching, coloring, and related problems.

importance.reason: A central historical efficiency question for local computation and consistent implicit graph solutions. It is resolved and therefore placed after unresolved candidates; the score records its significance rather than ongoing open status.

progress.text: The WOLA question records a Δ^(O(log log Δ)) polylog(n) bound and asks for poly(Δ,log n) probes.

Ghaffari’s Theorem 1.1 gives a polynomial-in-Δ per-vertex expected probe bound and a poly(Δ)·log(1/ε) tail bound with failure probability ε. Choosing ε inverse-polynomial in n yields the desired simultaneous bound by a union bound.
The result appears at FOCS 2022. The theorem also supplies a version using only poly(Δ log n) random bits. It explicitly leaves optimization of the degree exponent as a further direction.
Individual review matches the theorem’s model and guarantee to the saved 2019 existence question. This record is marked resolved affirmatively instead of remaining in the open-problem selection.

title: Polynomial-time detection of the seven-vertex tree H* as an induced minor — resolved
formal: Let H* have vertex set {a₁,a₂,b,c,d,e₁,e₂} and edge set {a₁b,a₂b,bc,cd,de₁,de₂}. Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that decides, for every finite simple undirected input graph G, whether H* is an induced minor of G? Answer: yes, by Eagling-Vose, Martin, Paulusma, and Trotignon (April 2026).
definitions: An induced-minor model is a family of seven nonempty, pairwise disjoint vertex sets Bₓ⊆V(G), indexed by x∈V(H*). Each induced subgraph G[Bₓ] must be connected. For every two distinct x,y, an edge of G joins Bₓ to Bᵧ if and only if xy is an edge of H*. Vertices outside the bags are discarded. Equivalently, H* is obtained by deleting vertices and contracting edges; arbitrary edge deletion is forbidden. Parallel edges and loops created inside contractions are suppressed to obtain a simple graph. The seven pattern vertices are names, not prescribed terminals in G. Bags can have unbounded size. H* is fixed and is not part of the input. The input is an adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph, with no promise of planarity, bounded degree, or exclusion of another induced subgraph. Polynomial time means at most C(n+1)^k elementary steps of a deterministic Turing machine, for fixed finite constants C and k. The question asks for membership in P, not the optimal polynomial exponent.
answer_criterion: A deterministic algorithm with a polynomial worst-case running time and correctness on every input answers yes. Theorem 17 of the April 2026 paper provides such an algorithm. The historical question is therefore closed; a smaller running-time exponent would be a separate question.
context:
The original Dagstuhl question specifies this particular seven-vertex tree: two degree-three branch vertices joined through a degree-two vertex, with two leaves at each branch vertex. Its generic saved title concealed this concrete target. Keeping the target fixed is essential: a classification for arbitrary patterns H is a larger problem, and the theorem closing this card does not settle that classification.

Ordinary minors permit deletion of inconvenient edges between bags. Induced minors must preserve every adjacency among the surviving bags, so connectivity alone is insufficient. Although H* has only seven vertices, trying all seven-vertex induced subgraphs does not decide the question: a valid bag can require many vertices of G. The branch-set definition makes the exact extra obstruction visible.

Fiala, Kamiński, and Paulusma developed algorithms for star-like induced minors in 2012. Their results covered all forests with at most seven vertices except this case. Thus H* isolated a small missing boundary in a much broader family of tractable containment problems, rather than an arbitrary choice of a graph with seven vertices.

The October 2025 version of Induced Minor Models II still identifies this tree as open. It expands several polynomial-time pattern families and proves tractability for any fixed pattern when the input excludes a fixed induced path. Those input-restricted results do not decide containment in an unrestricted graph.

The April 2026 solution first searches for models having a small branch bag. If none exists, a structural description permits a shortest-path detector to find the remaining models. The order of these steps matters: some auxiliary configurations are themselves hard to detect without the structural promise established by the first step. Together with earlier results, the solution completes polynomial-time detection for every forest on at most seven vertices.
why: This was the smallest unresolved forest-pattern case in induced-minor detection, a basic graph containment operation sitting between subgraph detection and ordinary minor detection. Its solution explains how forbidding unwanted cross-edges can remain algorithmically manageable. It is retained as a resolved historical benchmark, with its original identifier and source.

importance.reason: A historically important minimal missing case in a structural algorithm classification. The precise seven-vertex pattern has now been solved; its importance score records that role, while resolved status removes it from the active open-problem ordering.

progress.text: Star-like induced-minor algorithms establish polynomial-time detection for all forests on at most seven vertices except H*.
Paulusma explicitly asks for the complexity of detecting H* as an induced minor in Section 4.3 of the Dagstuhl report.
Induced Minor Models II still records the seven-vertex case as open while proving other fixed-pattern and restricted-input algorithms.

Theorem 17 gives a polynomial-time algorithm for the same pattern, denoted H₂ in the paper. Theorem 2 then covers every forest on at most seven vertices. The historical decision question has answer yes.

title: Succinct dynamic rank/select in a polynomial universe — resolved
formal: Can a dynamic set S⊆{0,…,U−1}, with n=|S| and polynomially larger universe U=n^(1+Θ(1)), be represented using H(n,U)+o(H(n,U)) bits while supporting insertion, deletion, rank and select in deterministic O(1+log n/log log(n+2)) worst-case time per operation on a word RAM with multiplication and word size Θ(log U)? Here H(n,U)=log₂ binom(U,n). Yes: Domingues’s 2026 construction implies this bound.
definitions: Fix any constants δ>0 and K≥1+δ. The bounds must hold uniformly whenever n≥2 and n^(1+δ)≤U≤n^K, with constants allowed to depend on δ,K. U is fixed during an operation sequence and n may change by one per update; both endpoints of each update are in the stated regime. Insert(x) adds an absent key, Delete(x) removes a present key, Rank(x)=|{y∈S:y≤x}| for any x∈{0,…,U−1}, and Select(j) returns the j-th smallest key for 1≤j≤n. Invalid select arguments return a failure symbol. These are set updates, not insertions that shift the positions of a bit string. The machine has w=⌈log₂(U+1)⌉-bit words and unit-cost reads/writes, comparisons, addition/subtraction, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts and word multiplication. All operations are exact, deterministic and terminating. Initialization from the initial set may take polynomial time in U. Space uses the M_B convention: unused gaps below the highest allocated address count, including partially used final words. Count all stored metadata and lookup tables; a fixed table of polylog(w) words computable from w is allowed and fits in the asymptotic redundancy here. No free input-dependent advice is provided. During an update use the larger of the pre- and post-update space budgets. Succinctness means that the redundancy divided by H(n,U) tends to zero uniformly over the fixed polynomial regime.
answer_criterion: The historical existence target is resolved affirmatively with deterministic worst-case operations. This does not assert o(n) redundancy at that same deterministic worst-case time, nor a bound for every universe density. The precise target is vanishing redundancy relative to H(n,U).
context:
Rank translates a key into its position in sorted order, while select translates a position back into a key. Together they support predecessor search and form an interface used inside compressed representations. A fully indexable dictionary must answer rank even when the queried key is absent, which is stronger than an index that only accepts stored keys.

There are binom(U,n) possible sets of a fixed cardinality, so H(n,U) bits is the basic information requirement. A conventional search tree also stores navigation information and counts, whose overhead can be substantial. Succinctness asks for a representation whose extra bits become a negligible fraction of that information requirement.

The word “succinct” needs its formula. In the polynomial-universe regime here, H is Θ(n log n). An overhead of n times a fractional power of log n is therefore succinct even though it exceeds n bits. The 2025 source uses relative redundancy as its definition; silently replacing that target by o(n) extra bits would create a stronger question.

Static indexing can inspect the entire set once and organize an elaborate compressed representation. Updates must preserve both the indexing information and the encoding as the set changes. The 2025 static FID result explicitly left the dynamic time-and-space combination as a separate question.

Two subsequent results address different guarantees. The SODA 2026 construction gets much smaller redundancy with amortized expected operation time. Domingues’s construction gives deterministic worst-case time with a larger but still negligible relative overhead. The latter directly answers the stronger time convention fixed in this card.
why: Rank/select is a basic ordered-data interface. Achieving its optimal dynamic time together with near-minimum encoding space shows that compression need not cost an additional asymptotic slowdown, and distinguishes space spent on information from space spent on navigation.

importance.reason: A basic time-space frontier for a widely used ordered-data primitive. The historical existence question is now resolved; its importance is preserved while resolved cards sort below open candidates.

progress.text: Liang and Zhou give optimal static FID trade-offs and explicitly leave succinct dynamic FIDs with O(log n/log log n) operation time open for polynomial universes. Their definition of succinctness is redundancy o(H), not necessarily o(n).

Kuszmaul, Liang, and Zhou give dynamic insert/delete/rank/select with optimal amortized expected time and redundancy n/2^((log n)^Ω(1))+polylog U in the polynomial regime. This addresses the earlier existence question with randomized amortized guarantees.

Domingues’s Theorem 1 gives deterministic worst-case O(1/ε+log_w n) operations with H+O(n w^ε/ε) bits and a polylog(w)-word table. The construction also supports selecting zero bits in the complement.

Set ε=1/4 and w=Θ(log U)=Θ(log n). The redundancy is O(n(log n)^(1/4))+polylog(log n), which is o(n log n)=o(H), and log_w n=Θ(log n/log log n). Thus the theorem supplies exactly the required deterministic worst-case succinct structure.

title: Multipass pairing heaps: logarithmic amortized delete-min — resolved
formal: Does the standard multipass pairing heap satisfy the following bound? For every valid operation sequence starting with no heaps, let D be the number of delete-min operations, Q the number of all other operations, and N the maximum size of any heap during the sequence. The total number of key comparisons and constant-time pointer operations is at most C[Q + D log₂(N+2)] for a universal C. Allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld and delete-min. The answer is yes, as a consequence of Sinnamon and Tarjan’s theorem.
definitions: Keys are opaque elements of a total order, with distinct keys for simplicity. A nonempty heap is one rooted ordered tree with each parent key smaller than its children’s keys; its root is the minimum. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger-key root the leftmost child of the smaller-key root. Insertion links a singleton with the existing root, or creates the root if empty. Melding consumes two disjoint heaps and links their roots, with empty heaps handled directly. find-min returns the root key. delete-min removes the root and treats its children, in their current left-to-right order, as roots. A pass links the first and second roots, the third and fourth, and so on; an unpaired final root carries over unchanged. The surviving roots remain in their relative order. Repeat complete passes from left to right until at most one root remains. Sibling lists and child pointers support each link in O(1) pointer operations. Valid delete-min and find-min calls use nonempty heaps. N=0 is allowed for sequences containing no inserted item. The bound is over the whole sequence, including a sequence ending with nonempty heaps. Decrease-key is excluded from this precise basic bound; its separate cost is discussed below.
answer_criterion: The historical target is the stated universal sequence bound for this exact pairing schedule. It has been proved. A single delete-min need not take O(log N) actual time; the logarithmic guarantee is amortized across the operation sequence.
context:
Self-adjusting heaps rearrange their trees in response to operations without storing balance ranks or subtree sizes. The multipass rule is especially simple: remove the minimum, pair adjacent roots repeatedly, and retain the smaller root in each pair. The absence of explicit balancing makes the implementation short, but conceals how much future work a link creates.

An individual minimum can have many children. Removing that root therefore may require a linear number of links, even though each pairing pass approximately halves the root list. Counting the number of passes alone does not prove a logarithmic operation cost. The analysis must account for links over an entire sequence.

The 2018 paper reduced the extra factor above logarithmic amortized cost to a very slowly growing expression involving the iterated logarithm. That was a meaningful improvement in the analysis, but it still did not give the exact logarithmic target. The same paper also studies path-balanced search trees; those are a separate algorithm and question.

Sinnamon and Tarjan subsequently obtained logarithmic amortized delete-min, constant-time insertion and melding, and stronger bounds that discount items never deleted. Their theorem also allows decrease-key operations, charging them separately. The displayed formulation keeps only the basic operations so that the claim about delete-min cannot accidentally promise free decrease-key.

This remains in the catalogue as a resolved historical card. It documents how a long-standing analysis problem was settled without changing the familiar multipass algorithm. Keeping the exact pairing order also prevents confusion with the standard two-pass pairing heap, whose second pass accumulates links differently.
why: The problem was a basic test of whether a simple restructuring rule gives optimal amortized priority-queue performance without balance metadata. Its solution supplies techniques for understanding other self-adjusting trees and separates the cost of deleting minima from the harder decrease-key analysis.

importance.reason: Historically fundamental analysis of a canonical self-adjusting priority queue. The logarithmic delete-min target is now resolved, so this historical importance score does not place it ahead of open candidates.

progress.text: Fredman, Sedgewick, Sleator, and Tarjan introduce pairing heaps and the multipass variant. The original multipass analysis leaves a slowly growing factor above logarithmic cost.

Dorfman and coauthors improve the multipass delete-min upper bound to O(log n · log* n · 2^(log* n)) and explicitly retain the logarithmic target as open. The saved excerpt occurs on printed page 24:3.

Sinnamon and Tarjan announce the logarithmic amortized delete-min bound. Their multipass decrease-key bound is O(log log n · log log log n), while slim and smooth heaps attain O(log log n). These are different guarantees for different heap variants.
The revised paper states the multipass sequence bound as Theorem 7.18. The work appears in ACM Transactions on Algorithms 21(4), Article 37, and resolves the historical question retained here.
